title: How One Man Controlled 90% of America's Oil
note: Narration lines use {shown|spoken} where the caption and the spoken form differ, e.g. {1870|eighteen seventy}.

shots.label: Washington, D.C.
say: In {1911|nineteen eleven}, the Supreme Court of the United States ordered one of the most powerful companies on earth to be broken into pieces.
It was meant to be a punishment.
Instead, by most estimates, it made its founder the richest American who has ever lived.

shots.title: Standard Oil
shots.sub: The rise and breakup of an empire
say: This is the story of Standard Oil.

shots.label: of America's oil refining
say: How a quiet bookkeeper from Cleveland took control of nearly {90%|ninety percent} of America's oil.
How he did it.
And why, when the government finally tore his empire apart, he walked away richer than ever.

shots.label: Richford, New York
say: John Davison Rockefeller was born in {1839|eighteen thirty-nine}, in a small town in upstate New York.
His father was a travelling salesman who sold doubtful medicines, and who was often gone for months at a time.
His mother was strict, religious, and careful with every cent.
The boy took after his mother.

shots.caption: Assistant bookkeeper, age 16
say: At sixteen, he found his first job, as an assistant bookkeeper at a small trading firm in Cleveland, Ohio.
He loved it. He loved the columns of figures, and the way a ledger showed exactly where every dollar went.
For the rest of his life he celebrated the day he was hired, the twenty-sixth of September, as a personal holiday.
He kept his own ledger too. Every cent earned, every cent spent, every cent given to his church.
It was a habit he never dropped.
At nineteen, he went into business for himself, trading grain, hay and meat.
He was careful, patient, and almost never surprised.

shots.label: About a hundred miles away
say: And later that same year, {1859|eighteen fifty-nine}, something happened about a hundred miles away that would change his life.

shots.caption: Titusville, Pennsylvania · August 1859
say: In August {1859|eighteen fifty-nine}, near the village of Titusville, Pennsylvania, a man named Edwin Drake drilled into the ground and struck oil.
It was the start of the first oil rush in America.

shots.caption: Oil meant light
say: At the time, oil was not about cars. There were no cars. Oil meant light.
Refined into kerosene, it burned brighter and cheaper than whale oil or candles, and it let ordinary families light their homes after dark.
Thousands of people rushed to Pennsylvania to drill.
Fortunes were made in a week and lost in a day. Prices swung wildly.
Rockefeller looked at the chaos and saw that drilling was a gamble.
Refining was a business.

shots.label: His first refinery, Cleveland
say: In {1863|eighteen sixty-three}, he invested in a refinery in Cleveland.

shots.label: to buy out his partners, at auction, in 1865
say: Two years later, he bought out his partners at auction, for {$72,500|seventy-two thousand five hundred dollars}.
He was twenty-five years old, and he now controlled one of the largest refineries in the city.

shots.label: Standard Oil is founded
say: In January {1870|eighteen seventy}, Rockefeller and his partners, among them Henry Flagler, created a new company.
They called it Standard Oil.
The name was a promise: kerosene of a standard quality, that customers could trust.

shots.label: of America's refining, in 1870
say: At its birth, Standard Oil handled about a tenth of America's oil refining.
Rockefeller wanted the rest.

shots.caption: Efficiency, taken to an extreme
say: His method was efficiency, taken to an extreme.
Standard made its own barrels. It bought its own forests for the wood.
It found uses for the leftovers that other refiners poured away. It counted costs to a fraction of a cent.

shots.caption: Secret discounts: the rebates
say: And then there were the railroads.
Oil had to travel by rail, and Standard shipped more of it than anyone.
So Rockefeller went to the railroads and demanded secret discounts, known as rebates.
The railroads agreed. Standard could now move oil more cheaply than any rival.
In {1872|eighteen seventy-two}, he turned that advantage into a weapon.
He visited his competitors in Cleveland, one by one, and made them an offer.
Sell to Standard Oil, for cash or for shares.
Or try to compete against a company that can ship for less than you ever will.

shots.label: Cleveland refiners sold to Standard Oil
say: Within a few months, twenty-two of his twenty-six Cleveland competitors had sold.
It became known as the Cleveland Massacre.
From Cleveland, Standard moved outward. Pittsburgh. Philadelphia. New York.
Refinery after refinery was bought, absorbed, or closed.

shots.caption: Then came the pipelines
say: When rivals built pipelines to escape the railroads, Standard built and bought pipelines of its own.

shots.label: of America's refining, by about 1880
say: By about {1880|eighteen eighty}, Standard Oil refined roughly {90%|ninety percent} of America's oil.

shots.label: The Standard Oil Trust · nine trustees
say: To hold it all together, Rockefeller's lawyers invented a new kind of structure.
In {1882|eighteen eighty-two}, the shareholders of dozens of companies handed their shares to nine trustees, led by Rockefeller.
It was called the Standard Oil Trust.
Here is the part that complicates the story.

shots.caption: The price of kerosene fell sharply
say: In these years, the price of kerosene fell sharply. Light became cheaper for millions of people.
Rockefeller's defenders said he had brought order and low prices to a wasteful industry.
His critics said he had done it by crushing every rival, in secret, and that no single man should hold that much power.
Both were telling the truth.

shots.label: The Sherman Antitrust Act
say: In {1890|eighteen ninety}, Congress passed the Sherman Antitrust Act, a law aimed squarely at combinations like Standard.
For years, it changed very little. The trust was reorganised as a holding company in New Jersey, and carried on.

shots.caption: Ida Tarbell, journalist
say: Then came a journalist. Her name was Ida Tarbell.
She had grown up in the oil region of Pennsylvania, where her father was one of the independent oil men squeezed by Standard's deals with the railroads.

shots.label: parts, in McClure's Magazine, from 1902
say: Beginning in {1902|nineteen oh two}, she published her investigation in McClure's Magazine, in nineteen parts.
Using court records, documents and interviews, she laid out exactly how Standard had been built.
The public was gripped. And angry.

shots.caption: United States v. Standard Oil
say: In {1906|nineteen oh six}, the federal government sued Standard Oil under the Sherman Act. The case took five years.
On the fifteenth of May, {1911|nineteen eleven}, the Supreme Court gave its ruling.
Standard Oil was an illegal monopoly. It had six months to break itself apart.

shots.label: separate companies
say: It was split into thirty-four separate companies.
And here is the twist.

shots.label: About a quarter of every piece
say: Rockefeller owned about a quarter of Standard Oil.
After the breakup, he owned about a quarter of each of the thirty-four pieces.

shots.caption: A new demand: gasoline
say: The timing could not have been better for him.
The automobile was arriving, and with it a huge new demand for a product that refiners had once treated as waste. Gasoline.
Freed from one another, the new companies grew fast, and their share prices soared.

shots.label: his estimated fortune, around 1913
say: Within a couple of years, Rockefeller's fortune was estimated at around {$900 million|nine hundred million dollars}.
That was roughly two percent of the entire American economy.

rows: Standard Oil of New Jersey → Exxon
Standard Oil of New York → Mobil
say: The pieces are still with us.
Standard Oil of New Jersey became Exxon.
Standard Oil of New York became Mobil.
Standard Oil of California became Chevron.

shots.label: Exxon and Mobil merge
say: In {1999|nineteen ninety-nine}, Exxon and Mobil merged back together.

lines: he had used to make it.
say: Rockefeller had stepped back from running the company years before the breakup.
He spent the second half of his life giving money away, with the same method he had used to make it.
He funded the University of Chicago, a medical research institute in New York, and the Rockefeller Foundation.

shots.label: given away in his lifetime
say: In all, he gave away more than {$500 million|five hundred million dollars}.
He died in {1937|nineteen thirty-seven}, at the age of ninety-seven.
So what is the lesson of Standard Oil?
Rockefeller did not win because he found oil. He never cared much for drilling.

shots.caption: The narrow point everyone must pass through
say: He won because he controlled the narrow point that everyone else had to pass through.
The refineries. The railroads. The pipelines.
Control the bottleneck, and you control the industry.
It was true of oil in {1880|eighteen eighty}. It is worth asking where it is true today.

shots.title: Behind the Fortune
shots.sub: The stories behind the world's great fortunes
say: This has been Behind the Fortune.
